vignette:
Linh is a 24-year-old Vietnamese-American woman working as an urban planner for a mid-sized city planning department. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 39 and a history of chronic physical abuse by her mother throughout childhood, which ended only when Linh left for college at eighteen. She has sought therapy now, she says quietly, because she is exhausted - not from any single crisis, but from the cumulative weight of a life spent bracing.

The abuse was not episodic in the way Linh imagines other people's traumas to be. It was woven into the ordinary texture of childhood: a hand shooting out across the dinner table, a grip on her arm during what looked, from the outside, like routine correction. What made it particularly corrosive was its bodily intimacy - her mother would grab her face to force eye contact, press her down onto surfaces, handle her as though she were an object to be repositioned rather than a child to be spoken to. Linh learned early that being seen - being looked at directly, being the focus of attention - preceded pain. She also learned that her body's signals, the nausea that rose before her mother's moods broke, were reliable warnings. Those two things, the sensation of being watched and the sick feeling in her stomach, became the nervous system's shorthand for danger.

Today, Linh's work requires her to present at public meetings, to stand at the front of conference rooms while colleagues and community members look at her. On those days the self-consciousness of being seen arrives not as social anxiety in any ordinary sense but as something older and more physical - her stomach turns, and with the nausea comes a fragmentary emotional surge, rage or dread, that feels entirely out of proportion to the room she is standing in. She cannot always retrieve a clear image of what the feeling belongs to; the memory surfaces as pure affect, a wave of intensity without an accompanying picture, which is itself disorienting. When she tries deliberately to recall specific incidents from childhood she finds the memories oddly inaccessible, blurred, as though behind frosted glass - yet the emotional force of them arrives unbidden and unannounced. This quality of her memory has made it harder, not easier, to process what happened: because she cannot narrate it cleanly, she has come to doubt the severity of it, which feeds directly into her belief that she is simply a weak person who cannot manage what others manage without difficulty.

That belief - that she is weak, that she is less than a person, that what was done to her was profoundly unjust and yet somehow also evidence of her own inadequacy - sits at the center of how Linh moves through the world. She has come to feel that she is an object in the hands of others, and this appraisal keeps her vigilance permanently elevated: she monitors her colleagues' body language with exhausting precision, and a sudden movement from someone nearby - a hand raised to gesture, a chair pushed back - puts her immediately on guard, her attention narrowing to that movement as though it were the only thing in the room. The hypervigilance in turn contracts her sense of safety until it covers almost no territory at all; she feels genuinely at ease only in her own apartment, and even there the ease is conditional. Living at that constant pitch of alertness, Linh found the world had grown dense with signals she could not stop reading - already running on threat, almost anything could tip into a warning: a colleague's gaze held a fraction too long, a hand raised to gesture, the particular quality of nausea rising in her stomach before a presentation. The background hum of danger she carried everywhere meant these ordinary cues arrived pre-loaded with urgency, each one confirming what her nervous system already believed.

Because being seen triggers both the somatic alarm and the memory's emotional residue, Linh has organized her life around minimizing exposure. She goes along with whatever her colleagues suggest in meetings, never volunteering a position of her own, because disagreement feels like an invitation to become a target. Yet the avoidance had drawn its own map of the trauma around her: every meeting she deflected, every medical appointment she cancelled, every conversation she redirected had become a marker in itself - a daily, wordless acknowledgement of what her body still considered dangerous. The routes she no longer took and the things she could no longer say had quietly multiplied, until the cues she was trying to escape seemed to be everywhere she looked. This people-pleasing has cost her professionally - her supervisor has noted, with puzzlement, that Linh's written work is sophisticated but she rarely advocates for her own proposals. She also avoids any conversation in which someone might reference her childhood, redirecting or leaving the room, which means she has never told anyone close to her what happened. The avoidance quiets the immediate alarm but keeps the memory sealed, preventing any reworking of it, and so the rage and the sense of injustice remain as raw as they were years ago. Because she had never stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her nervous system had never received the evidence it needed - the threat remained as high as the day it was first set, and her safety behaviours, by their very persistence, confirmed to some part of her that the danger they were guarding against must be real and ongoing. Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was, and so the avoidance sealed that possibility off entirely. She has also stopped attending routine medical appointments, because the examination table, the clinical handling of her body, returns her instantly to the sensation of being managed without consent.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a mandatory physical examination required by her employer's health insurance renewal. She lay on the examination table, a stranger's hands moving efficiently across her, and felt - not fear exactly, but a total, annihilating certainty that she did not exist as a person in that room. She wept in her car afterward for an hour and could not explain why. What she most hopes for, she says, is to stop feeling like something that happened to her body rather than someone who lives in it.
